proofs.proof_tex:
Put \(w(r)=\omega_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}}(r)\).  By
\(\mathrm{lem{:}total\text{-}modulus\text{-}rule}\), \(w\) is finite,
nondecreasing, and concave, and the canonical endpoints satisfy
\(x_r^+-x_r^-=h_r\) and
\(\ell(x_r^+)-\ell(x_r^-)=w(r)\).  We first verify that radius one belongs
to \(\mathcal R_+\).  Let \(e=(\mathbf 1_T,0)\).  Adding a scalar multiple
of \(e\) to an element of \(2\mathcal M_{T,m}\) preserves all Holder
difference inequalities, all bounds on the deviation coordinates, and all
calendar-centering equalities, by
\(\mathrm{def{:}model\text{-}class}\).  Moreover,
\(\ell(e)=1\) by \(\mathrm{def{:}target\text{-}functional}\), while
\(Ke=\mathbf 1_O\ne0\) by
\(\mathrm{def{:}observation\text{-}operator}\).  The set \(O\) is nonempty
by \(\mathrm{ass{:}index\text{-}range}\) and
\(\mathrm{ass{:}terminal\text{-}range}\).  If the maximizer \(h_1\)
had \(\|Kh_1\|_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}^{-1}}<1\), continuity of the norm
would therefore make \(h_1+a e\) feasible for all sufficiently small
\(a>0\), although \(\ell(h_1+a e)=\ell(h_1)+a\), a contradiction.
Consequently \(\|Kh_1\|_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}^{-1}}=1\).

The same constant direction gives
\[
 w(r)\ge
 \frac{r}{\|\mathbf 1_O\|_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}^{-1}}},
 \qquad r>0,
\]
so \(w\) is unbounded.  If its nonnegative right derivative at any positive
radius were zero, concavity would force every subsequent secant slope to be
nonpositive; monotonicity would then make \(w\) constant thereafter.  This
would contradict the preceding display.  Hence
\(s:=w'_+(1)>0\), and radius one is in \(\mathcal R_+\).

The supergradient inequality at one, evaluated at zero, gives
\(w(0)\le w(1)-s\).  Since \(w(0)\ge0\),
\[
 0\le b:=\frac{w(1)-s}{2}\le\frac{w(1)}2,
 \qquad 0<s\le w(1).
\]
By \(\mathrm{lem{:}total\text{-}modulus\text{-}rule}\), \(b\) is the
maximal absolute bias of \(\widehat\theta_1\), and its standard deviation is
\(s\).  Therefore
\[
 \sup_{x\in\mathcal M_{T,m}}
 \mathbb E_x[(\widehat\theta_1-\ell(x))^2]
 \le b^2+s^2\le\frac54w(1)^2.
\]
The defining inequality for \(r_{\mathrm{MSE},j}\) now yields
\[
 \liminf_{j\to\infty}\sup_x
 \mathbb E_x[
   \{\widehat\theta_{r_{\mathrm{MSE},j}}-\ell(x)\}^2
 ]
 \le \inf_{r\in\mathcal R_+}(b_r^2+s_r^2)
 \le \frac54w(1)^2.
\]
Since \(R^\star\) is the infimum over all sample-measurable estimators by
\(\mathrm{def{:}risk\text{-}and\text{-}length}\), it is no larger than
each displayed worst-case risk and hence no larger than their lower limit.

For the converse, take the canonical endpoints \(x_1^-\) and \(x_1^+\).
By \(\mathrm{lem{:}score\text{-}covariance}\), their data laws
\(P_-\) and \(P_+\) are Gaussian with their common positive-definite
covariance \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}\), mean difference \(Kh_1\), and target
separation \(\Delta=w(1)\).  If
\(d^2=\|Kh_1\|_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}^{-1}}^2\le1\), direct integration of
the Gaussian likelihood ratio gives
\[
 \chi^2(P_+,P_-)
 =\mathbb E_-\!\left[
   \left\{\frac{dP_+}{dP_-}-1\right\}^2
 \right]
 =e^{d^2}-1\le e-1.
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz applied to
\(\operatorname{TV}(P_+,P_-)=\frac12\mathbb E_-|dP_+/dP_--1|\)
therefore gives
\(\operatorname{TV}(P_+,P_-)\le\frac12\sqrt{e-1}\).

For an arbitrary estimator, decide for the endpoint whose target value is
closer to its reported value.  On either testing-error event the squared
estimation error is at least \(\Delta^2/4\).  The sum of the two testing-error
probabilities is at least \(1-\operatorname{TV}(P_+,P_-)\), by the defining
variational inequality for total variation.  Thus
\[
 \max_{\nu\in\{-,+\}}
 \mathbb E_\nu[(\widetilde\theta-\ell(x_1^\nu))^2]
 \ge \frac{\Delta^2}{8}
 \{1-\operatorname{TV}(P_+,P_-)\}
 \ge
 \frac{1-\frac12\sqrt{e-1}}8w(1)^2.
\]
Both endpoints belong to \(\mathcal M_{T,m}\), so taking the infimum over
estimators proves the lower bound.  Every constant in the argument is
independent of \(N,T,m,q,L,B,\beta\), which proves the asserted uniformity.

Fix \(j\), abbreviate \(r=r_{\mathrm{CI},j}\), \(b=b_r\), and \(s=s_r>0\),
and let
\(a_x=\mathbb E_x[\widehat\theta_r]-\ell(x)\).  By
\(\mathrm{lem{:}score\text{-}covariance}\), the estimator is Gaussian.
By \(\mathrm{lem{:}total\text{-}modulus\text{-}rule}\), its standard
deviation is exactly \(s\) and \(|a_x|\le b\) for every
\(x\in\mathcal M_{T,m}\).  Hence
\[
 \frac{\widehat\theta_r-\ell(x)}s
 \sim\mathcal N(t_x,1),
 \qquad t_x=a_x/s,
 \qquad |t_x|\le b/s.
\]
For \(c\ge0\) and \(t\ge0\), set
\(g_c(t)=\Pr\{|\mathcal N(t,1)|\le c\}
=\Phi(c-t)+\Phi(c+t)-1\).  Its derivative is
\(g_c'(t)=\phi(c+t)-\phi(c-t)\le0\), because
\((c+t)^2\ge(c-t)^2\).  Symmetry gives \(g_c(t)=g_c(-t)\).
The definition of \(\operatorname{cv}_\alpha\) therefore implies
\[
 \Pr_x\!\left{
   |\widehat\theta_r-\ell(x)|
   \le s\operatorname{cv}_\alpha(b/s)
 \right}
 \ge1-\alpha.
\]
This is the asserted finite-sample uniform coverage.  The half-length is
deterministic and equals
\(s_r\operatorname{cv}_\alpha(b_r/s_r)\); its factor
\(1+j^{-1}\) inequality is exactly the defining inequality for
\(r_{\mathrm{CI},j}\) in
\(\mathrm{def{:}affine\text{-}estimator}\).

Let \(z_\alpha=\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha/2)\).  For every \(t\ge0\), the interval
\([-t-z_\alpha,t+z_\alpha]\) contains
\([t-z_\alpha,t+z_\alpha]\), so
\(\Pr\{|\mathcal N(t,1)|\le t+z_\alpha\}\ge1-\alpha\).  Thus
\(\operatorname{cv}_\alpha(t)\le t+z_\alpha\).  We next verify directly
that radius one is admissible.  With \(e=(\mathbf 1_T,0)\), adding \(ae\)
preserves membership in \(2\mathcal M_{T,m}\), because it changes none of
the Holder differences or deviation coordinates.  The set \(O\) is
nonempty by \(\mathrm{ass{:}index\text{-}range}\) and
\(\mathrm{ass{:}terminal\text{-}range}\).  Since \(\ell(e)=1\) and
\(Ke=\mathbf 1_O\ne0\), a radius-one maximizer with slack Mahalanobis norm
could be improved by adding a sufficiently small positive multiple of
\(e\).  Hence its norm constraint is active.  The same direction shows that
\(w\) is unbounded; concavity and monotonicity then imply \(w'_+(1)>0\),
since a zero right derivative would make \(w\) constant thereafter.  Thus
\(1\in\mathcal R_+\).  The supergradient inequality at one gives
\(w(0)\le w(1)-s_1\), where \(s_1=w'_+(1)\).  Therefore
\(0<s_1\le w(1)\) and \(b_1=\{w(1)-s_1\}/2\ge0\).  Consequently
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 2s_1\operatorname{cv}_\alpha(b_1/s_1)
 &\le 2b_1+2z_\alpha s_1\\
 &=w(1)+(2z_\alpha-1)s_1\\
 &\le \{1+2z_\alpha\}w(1).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Using the infimum-approaching property of \(r_{\mathrm{CI},j}\) and the
fact that the interval length is nonrandom gives
\[
 \liminf_{j\to\infty}\sup_x
 \mathbb E_x[\operatorname{length}C_{\alpha,j}(Z)]
 \le \{1+2z_\alpha\}w(1).
\]
Every \(C_{\alpha,j}\) is admissible in the definition of
\(\operatorname{EL}^\star_\alpha\), so that definition also gives the
middle inequality.

It remains to prove the lower bound for every uniformly honest interval,
not merely for affine intervals.  Set
\[
 r_\alpha=\sqrt{\log\{1+(1-2\alpha)^2\}}.
\]
Because \(0<1-2\alpha<1\), one has \(0<r_\alpha<\sqrt{\log2}<1\).
Take the canonical endpoints \(x^-_{r_\alpha},x^+_{r_\alpha}\), whose
target separation is \(\Delta_\alpha=w(r_\alpha)\).  The same direct
Gaussian likelihood-ratio calculation as above yields
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(P_+,P_-)
 \le\frac12\sqrt{e^{r_\alpha^2}-1}
 =\frac{1-2\alpha}{2}.
\]
If \(C\) is any interval with coverage at least \(1-\alpha\) at both
endpoints, then, under \(P_-\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Pr_-\{\ell(x^-_{r_\alpha}),\ell(x^+_{r_\alpha})\in C\}
 &\ge 1-2\alpha-\operatorname{TV}(P_+,P_-)\\
 &\ge\frac{1-2\alpha}{2}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
On this event the interval has length at least \(\Delta_\alpha\).  Hence
\[
 \sup_x\mathbb E_x[\operatorname{length}C]
 \ge\frac{1-2\alpha}{2}w(r_\alpha).
\]
Finally, concavity and nonnegativity give
\[
 w(r_\alpha)
 \ge r_\alpha w(1)+(1-r_\alpha)w(0)
 \ge r_\alpha w(1).
\]
Taking the infimum over all uniformly honest intervals proves
\(\operatorname{EL}^\star_\alpha\ge c_\alpha w(1)\), where
\(c_\alpha=(1-2\alpha)r_\alpha/2\).  The constants depend only on
\(\alpha\), so the conclusion is uniform over the full stated design range.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed:
For every \(j\in\mathbb N\), the interval \(C_{\alpha,j}(Z)\) has exact finite-sample uniform coverage
\[
 \inf_{x\in\mathcal M_{T,m}}
 \Pr_x\{\ell(x)\in C_{\alpha,j}(Z)\}\ge 1-\alpha.
\]
Its deterministic half-length satisfies
\[
 s_{r_{\mathrm{CI},j}}

   b_{r_{\mathrm{CI},j}}/s_{r_{\mathrm{CI},j}}
 \right)
 \le (1+j^{-1})

 s_r\operatorname{cv}_{\alpha}(b_r/s_r).

\[
 c_\alpha\omega_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}}(1)
 \le \operatorname{EL}^{\star}_{\alpha}
 \le \liminf_{j\to\infty}\sup_{x\in\mathcal M_{T,m}}
 \mathbb E_x[\operatorname{length}C_{\alpha,j}(Z)]
 \le
 \{1+2\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha/2)\}
 \omega_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}}(1).
\]

prose_updates.tldr: A fixed-cohort repeated-cross-section event study induces an exact Gaussian score experiment with shrinking not-yet-treated pools and nested shared-baseline dependence. For the causal terminal calendar ATT, the finite-dimensional covariance-weighted modulus \(\omega_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}}(1)\) now gives the operator-specific frontier: global minimax MSE is bounded above and below by explicit universal multiples of its square, and shortest uniformly honest expected length is bounded by explicit \(\alpha\)-dependent multiples of the modulus. Total measurable affine estimators and bias-aware intervals attain the upper bounds, with exact finite-sample coverage. The matched-date-block calculation remains a separate \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{diag}}\) calibration. Converting the nested modulus to the candidate closed-form calendar functional is open because the proposed dimension-free bounded lift is impossible.

project_justification.gap: Staggered-DiD work explains why valid long-run comparisons disappear, while Gaussian optimal-recovery theory begins with a supplied observation operator and covariance. Neither literature derives the exact nested shared-baseline score geometry and states the resulting global MSE and honest-length frontier for a terminal causal calendar ATT.
project_justification.niche: The contribution is the exact operator-specific inference problem generated by fixed cohort-stratified repeated cross sections: a computable finite-dimensional nested covariance modulus, rather than an unsupported scalar phase approximation.
project_justification.fill: The project derives the Gaussian score covariance, proves explicit two-point lower bounds and affine upper bounds for global minimax MSE and honest expected length, supplies a total bias-aware interval with exact coverage, and isolates conversion of the exact modulus to a closed-form calendar rate as the remaining mathematical question.

sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: No nuisance function is estimated inside the exact known-covariance score experiment. The Holder calendar path and bounded centered cohort deviations define one convex parameter class, and the estimator is computed from a finite-dimensional covariance-weighted modulus optimization.

prose_updates.related_work: Callaway and Sant'Anna supply the group-time causal effects and calendar aggregation underlying the target. Borusyak, Jaravel, and Spiess show in Section 3.3, Proposition 5, why sufficiently long-run effects lose valid comparisons, motivating extrapolation but not providing its inference frontier. Donoho's 1994 Gaussian model in equation (1), Theorem 1, and Section 11 supplies general modulus and affine-minimax architecture conditional on known operators and weights. Armstrong and Kolesar's 2018 Section 3.2, equations (23)--(26), develops bias-aware Gaussian intervals for supplied regression operators, and their 2020 equation (15) and Theorem 3.1 on pages 15--16 give a direct-regression Holder calibration. None of those results derives a bounded right inverse for the shared-baseline Gram term. The present contribution therefore stops at the exact nested modulus frontier. The matched-date-block proposition concerns only \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{diag}}\) and does not order or approximate the nested experiment.
prose_updates.interpretation: The exact modulus is actionable: for the observed calendar and cohort shares, solve its finite-dimensional convex optimization, use the exposed direction in the stated affine estimator, and report the corresponding bias-aware interval. Its value measures all smoothness, cohort-heterogeneity, and shared-baseline effects jointly. The candidate scalar functional \(\rho_{N,T,m}\) may be useful diagnostically, but no proved uniform equivalence licenses it as the nested-experiment rate.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: A dimension-free lift matching Holder localization, bounded-deviation leverage, and shared-baseline Mahalanobis energy cannot satisfy the claimed \(T/k^2\) energy bound already for equal shares, \(m=1\), and \(k=\lfloor T^{3/4}\rfloor\). Consequently the exact nested modulus has no proved closed-form calendar rate or phase diagram here. The matched comparison deletes only cross-date dependence after preserving each full within-date covariance block; it is a \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{diag}}\) sanity experiment and cannot be transferred to \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}\). The Gaussian model also leaves non-Gaussian coupling, nuisance estimation, and smoothness adaptation outside the present guarantee.
prose_updates.honest_scope: Established results are the exact score covariance, total measurable modulus procedures, explicit global MSE and honest-length comparisons with \(\omega_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}}(1)\), exact finite-sample interval coverage, and the separate matched-date-block calculation. No bounded right inverse, equivalence with \(\rho_{N,T,m}\), nested homogeneous rate, or closed-form nested phase diagram is claimed. Whether the exact nested modulus admits another useful calendar-scale characterization remains open; the adaptation question must respect that unresolved conversion.
